title: 道德經 第四十六章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 46, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 75. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 46 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 儉欲 (Sparing of Desire). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
天下有道，
卻走馬以糞。

morph.gloss: all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
to send back, to turn back, to return a thing whence it came
the fast horses — the post-horses kept for despatches and for war
to run — the classical sense; it does NOT mean 'to walk'
so as to, in order to — it hangs a purpose on what went before
dung; as a verb, to dung a field, to manure it

sentences.l:
All under heaven having the Way:
send the running horses back, so as to dung the fields.
sentences.i: When all under heaven holds to the Way, the fast horses are sent back to dung the fields.
sentences.n:
走 is the first trap in reading old Chinese: in the classical language it means to run, not to walk. 走馬 is one word, and it is the fast horses — the ones kept saddled for despatches and for war. Sending them back to tread manure into a field is the whole picture of a world with nothing to fight about.

Neither clause has a subject. The first is a bare condition — 'all under heaven having the Way' — with no 'when' and no 'if'; the second is a bare imperative or general statement with nobody named as doing it. English has to supply both, and every supplying is a small interpretation.

糞 is dung, and as a verb to put dung on the ground. Its object is left out; Wang Bi fills it in as 治田糞, to work and manure the fields, and 'the fields' in the literal is his supplying, not the text's.

sentences.t:
天下無道，
戎馬生於郊。

morph.gloss: all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
war-horses — the horses of a campaign
to be born; to give birth, to foal
the preposition standing after its verb — here 'in, out in'
the open country outside the city wall; hence the border, where armies stand

sentences.l:
All under heaven lacking the Way:
war-horses foal out in the borderland.
sentences.i: When the Way is gone from under heaven, war-horses are foaled on the frontier.
sentences.n:
The two units are one sentence with the middle taken out — same frame, opposite condition, and no connective at all to join them. This bare pairing is the book's commonest way of arguing.

郊 is the ground beyond the wall: not wilderness, but the open country where a city stops and where an army camps. A mare dropping her foal there is a precise image, not a general lament — the campaign has run so long that the breeding stock is in the field and nothing has come home. Wang Bi reads it as the outward face of greed: wanting without end, nothing tended within, everything sought outside.

於 is a preposition that follows its verb rather than preceding it — the reverse of the other Chinese prepositions, which go in front of the verb — and it takes whatever sense the line needs: here plain location.

sentences.t:
禍莫大於不知足；
咎莫大於欲得。
故知足之足，
常足矣。

morph.gloss: disaster, ruin that falls on one
nothing, none — a negative that carries its own subject
than — 於 after an adjective makes the comparison
a fault, blame — and the trouble a fault brings down
the genitive particle: 'of' — it makes a noun of 知足
enough — now a noun: the sufficiency itself
sentence-final particle: the matter has now come out — 'and there it is'

sentences.l:
Of disasters, none greater than not knowing enough;
of faults, none greater than wanting to get.
Therefore the enough of knowing-enough
abidingly is enough.
sentences.i: There is no ruin greater than not knowing what is enough, and no fault greater than wanting to get. So the sufficiency that comes of knowing what is enough is a sufficiency that abides.
sentences.n:
The 莫 … 於 comparison, first time in the book, and it has no word for 'more'. 莫 is a negative carrying its own subject — 'nothing, none' — and 於 after the plain adjective 大 supplies 'than': 禍莫大於 X, 'of disasters none is great beyond X'. The adjective alone does what English needs 'greater' for.

知足 is the chapter's coin, and the last two lines spend it three times in six characters: 知足 'to know enough' as a verb phrase, 之 turning that into a noun, and 足 again as the noun it yields. The sufficiency of knowing-sufficiency — the point being that it is a different thing from having a sufficiency, and unlike a sufficiency of goods it cannot be spent.

常 is the same 常 as chapter 1's 常道, the abiding; here it stands adverbially in front of 足. 矣 closes the chapter by marking the case as now settled.

The witnesses differ here. The Guodian bamboo slips and the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, and some received printings too, carry a third member ahead of these two — on 罪, crime, and desiring too much — which this text does not have. Guodian also writes the comparisons with 乎 where this text has 於; the two particles do the same job. Whether the third member dropped out here or was added there is not something the manuscripts settle.
